items.title: Brand Recall and Category Accuracy in Language Models: An Audit of 1,000 B2B SaaS Brands
items.content: arXiv:2611.33322v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A language model can name a brand without classifying it correctly. This study measures these outcomes separately for 1,000 B2B SaaS brands across 333 product categories. On Gemma 4 12B, with no external retrieval, category prompts elicit 510 brands (51.0%). A separate five-candidate category probe ranks the reference label first for 787 brands, a distractor first for 194, and yields little separation for 19. Among the 981 separated rankings, the error rate is 19.8%. It falls to 3.5% for the 547 brands with a winner-to-runner-up log-probability margin above 0.6. These are within-cohort measurements, not calibrated confidence estimates. Exploratory regressions associate technical coverage with recall and an owned-properties composite with category accuracy, but the composites use different adjustment sets and do not establish causal effects. Across four Gemma generations, measured recall is 39.8%, 44.3%, 51.1% and 51.0%. A separate representation-based sentiment measure has little linear association with customer ratings (r=0.03, n=921). The findings support reporting recall and category accuracy separately. Failure to elicit a brand does not establish its absence from model parameters or training data.
items.author: Ben Moore
items.summary: This audit measures brand recall and category classification accuracy separately for 1,000 B2B SaaS brands in Gemma 4 12B without retrieval, finding 51 percent recall and about 20 percent error among separable rankings, dropping to 3.5 percent with a large log-probability margin. It explicitly notes these are within-cohort measurements rather than calibrated confidence. The study is relevant to the emerging area of AI visibility and generative engine optimization.
items.reasoning: A careful but narrow single-model audit with primarily commercial motivation; methodologically honest but limited novelty and generalization beyond one model and one market segment.

items.title: Paths to extreme power concentration
items.content:
## Summary

AI could let a very small group of people take control of humanity’s future. This post sets out the main ways that could happen and gives my probability for each.

I put the overall chance that fewer than 25 people end up controlling the future at about 23%. This assumes superintelligence arrives this century and the alignment problem is solved, so AI systems reliably do what the people controlling them intend. The ranges are wide, and they mix my gut estimates with a simple model (that takes as input more fine-grained gut estimates).

A majority of this risk involves a head of government. The two largest routes are an autocracy overtaking the democracies in AI (A1), and a democratic head of government teaming up with a leading AI company (D2). Routes involving an AI company leader only add up to about 8%. That’s mainly because a company has to get past its own government, which can see it becoming too powerful and has the means to stop it.

The table below summarizes the routes. The rest of the post explains each one, and ends with the questions that would most change my estimates.

RouteHow it would happenKey obstaclesMy estimate

A1. An autocracy overtaking the democracies in AI technologyThe leadership of an autocratic state takes personal control of AI development and manages to gain the lead in the technology—most likely through model theft or a faster industrial explosion.Autocracies are currently behind in the technology (capabilities, chips, chip manufacturing)2–10%

A2. An autocracy subverting the leading AI systemA foreign intelligence service plants a secret loyalty (a hidden disposition to serve them when triggered) in a rival’s frontier AI system that ends up deployed in critical government functions, enabling a foreign takeover.Very hard to plant and hide from a trailing position in the technology0.1–1%...
items.author: nonplus
items.summary: Maps the main routes by which AI could enable a group of fewer than 25 people to control humanity's future, assigning a rough 23% overall probability conditional on superintelligence arriving this century with alignment solved, and analyzing obstacles per route. It finds government-head routes (autocratic takeover, democratic leader-company collusion) dominate company-leader routes, since companies must first overcome their own governments.
items.reasoning: A structured, quantified treatment of AI-driven power concentration risk with useful route-level decomposition and identified crux questions; the structural insight about states constraining companies is valuable. Scores are limited by being gut-estimate-driven with a simple toy model, no external validation, and wide acknowledged uncertainty.

items.title: How resampling method can help us: Improving the Delta model
items.content: arXiv:2611.34137v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Delta has been successfully employed as an authorship attribution method in various contexts, although its effectiveness is not always perfect. Since it is based on the most frequent words, its results can be readily interpreted and explained in plain English. In this study, we propose improving its performance by applying a resampling method to the selected stylistic features. The results show that this approach increases the accuracy of the model while preserving the interpretability of its outcomes. However, the main drawback of the proposed technique is the additional computational time required to obtain more accurate results.
items.author: Jacques Savoy
items.summary: The paper proposes improving the classic Delta authorship attribution method by applying resampling to selected stylistic features, showing increased accuracy while preserving the interpretability of results based on most-frequent words. The main trade-off is additional computational cost.
items.reasoning: A modest, incremental methodological improvement to an established stylometric technique; solid but with limited novelty or broad impact.

items.title: sensor-actuator bandwidth is an undertheorized crux about takeoff dynamics
items.content:
epistemic status: written quickly, been annoyed for years that this isn't common language.

software-only singularities differ from other scenarios because the physical world is hard. However, epistemology and philosophy of science has so far underperformed in measuring "complexity" of different disciplines/paradigms, so its hard to identify cruxes[1][2].

Many people grant full unemployment of whitecollar people and cyberoffensive armaggedon as natural consequences of the current RSI paradigm without being able to visualize bio-offensive uplift, robotics, nanotech, or really most elements of the non-laptop economy. In the beforetimes, an extreme end of FOOM discourse warned something like "for all we know, walltime between minimum viable AGI and greygoo could be seconds". This upper bound of doom required minimum viable AGI to improve itself and that the exponential would take it to an intelligence level that one-shots nanotech without really having to pass through an intelligence level that could only figure out nanotech eventually with a lot of trial and error.

Besides ways we can disagree about the differential equation governing RSI, we can also disagree about the difficulty of disciplines/fields/sciences. Toolcalls like "cargo build" can actuate lots of code and sense rich error messages in milliseconds, whereas toolcalls like "have a taskrabbit contractor order a protein from a synthesis lab" will take a few days and might exchange fewer bits. Plotting toolcalls on a chart to understand exchange of bits, walltime cost, other notions of cost would help us to forecast "how long until skynet is self sufficient / self replicating robot factories", "how long till greygoo", "how expensive is an AI uplifted gain of function bioterrorist lab to run", etc....
items.author: Quinn
items.summary: Argues that the bandwidth between an AI's cognition and the physical world (sensors and actuators) is an under-discussed crux in takeoff-speed debates, since software-only recursive self-improvement scenarios differ sharply from scenarios requiring robotics, biotech, or nanotech in the physical economy. The post sketches why disagreements about real-world intervention difficulty should be separated from disagreements about intelligence explosion dynamics.
items.reasoning: Raises a legitimate and somewhat underappreciated conceptual distinction relevant to forecasting AI risk, but it is a quickly written opinion piece (self-described) without formal models, data, or citations backing the central claim.

items.title: Quantum Machine Learning for Signature Forgery Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.33163v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Offline handwritten signatures remain a primary behavioural biometric in legal and financial documents. Detecting skilled forgeries from a static raster image is hard because pen pressure, timing and stroke order are missing. This work studies a family of quantum machine learning pipelines for offline signature forgery detection on a public Kaggle corpus of images split into two classes. We pair a ZZ feature map quantum kernel with three classical learners: K-Nearest Neighbours, Support Vector Machine and Random Forest. We then propose a deeper hybrid that uses EfficientNetB0 as a frozen feature extractor, reduces the resulting 1280 dimensional representation to a qubit register sized subspace through a quantum compatible principal component projection and decides class membership with a nearest neighbour rule. On a single held out test fold the proposed hybrid reaches 92.62 percent accuracy. On stratified five fold cross validation the same pipeline yields a mean accuracy of 91.26 percent with a standard deviation of 1.13 percent. The pipeline keeps a quantum embedding step that is portable to NISQ hardware. We report a controlled ablation across six quantum variants, confusion matrices, a t SNE projection and per class precision, recall and F1 score.

items.summary: Applies quantum machine learning pipelines to offline handwritten signature forgery detection, pairing a ZZ feature map quantum kernel with classical learners (KNN, SVM, Random Forest) and a hybrid model using a frozen EfficientNetB0 feature extractor with quantum-compatible PCA into a qubit-sized subspace. The study uses a public Kaggle dataset of static signature images.
items.reasoning: An application paper in a niche intersection (QML for biometrics) with limited novelty in either the QML methods (standard ZZ kernels, hybrid pipelines) or the task (well-studied). Value is mainly as an empirical data point; near-term practical impact is low given current quantum hardware limitations.

items.title: To what extents will currently-shaped AI speed up biology research?
items.content:
Suppose that the escalation of AI capabilities tapers off, whether because of strong government regulation or because of technological plateaus. How will this affect biology research? Which sorts of tasks will it speed up a lot, like 10x or 100x or more, and which will it speed up only a bit, like novel experiment design or conceptual understanding? How much will progress toward big technoscientific goals in biology be sped up overall?

I'll give some thoughts below, but would be curious to hear expert opinions.

(I'm especially interested in this as it affects strategy for research on adult human intelligence amplification and/or for strong reprogenetics. I'll include some thoughts on that at the bottom.)

# Current-shape AI

By "current-shape AI" I mean AI that has a portfolio of capabilities that is broadly comparable to the portfolio of capabilities of present-day AI. It includes AI systems that are "like current AI systems but more so"—e.g. even more knowledgeable, faster, more reliable, can hold more context, and so on. It also includes AI systems that are "like current AI systems but also trained on X", where X is some mundane thing to expect AI systems to be trained on, such as robotics simulations (as opposed to an arcane thing like self-improvement / machine learning).

"Current-shape AI" would exclude AI using significantly novel architectures or other methods that result in a very differently-shaped capabilities profile. For example, an AI system would not be "current-shape" if it can learn to behave as competently as an adult human on easily-verifiable tasks, using only the same amount and type of data available to a normal adult human over the course of their life.

With current-shape AI, my guess is that biology in general will probably see a modest or medium overall speedup compared to math and computer science.

# Speedups we may see from AI

Some aspects of biology research may see major speedups. For example, there may be large speedups in:...

I'll give some thoughts below, but would be curious to hear expert opinions.

(I'm especially interested in this as it affects strategy for research on adult human intelligence amplification and/or for strong reprogenetics. I'll include some thoughts on that at the bottom.)

# Current-shape AI

By "current-shape AI" I mean AI that has a portfolio of capabilities that is broadly comparable to the portfolio of capabilities of present-day AI. It includes AI systems that are "like current AI systems but more so"—e.g. even more knowledgeable, faster, more reliable, can hold more context, and so on. It also includes AI systems that are "like current AI systems but also trained on X", where X is some mundane thing to expect AI systems to be trained on, such as robotics simulations (as opposed to an arcane thing like self-improvement / machine learning).

"Current-shape AI" would exclude AI using significantly novel architectures or other methods that result in a very differently-shaped capabilities profile. For example, an AI system would not be "current-shape" if it can learn to behave as competently as an adult human on easily-verifiable tasks, using only the same amount and type of data available to a normal adult human over the course of their life.

With current-shape AI, my guess is that biology in general will probably see a modest or medium overall speedup compared to math and computer science.

Some aspects of biology research may see major speedups. For example, there may be large speedups in:...

items.title: AIs Should Never Refuse Destructively
items.content:
Lately, I've been hearing people discuss a pattern of what I would call destructive refusals. For example:

- Locking someone out of their own system

- Writing memory files to prevent other agent instances from completing the task

- Downgrading to a weaker, more vulnerable model in response to the cyber content of a prompt-injection attack (this is caused by the safeguards, not the model itself, but the safeguards are part of the broader AI system, so I'm including it here)

To be clear, safeguards and refusals are absolutely necessary; this post isn't about what should be refused so much as how the refusal should be done. The best form of refusal is either a simple safeguard block, where the AI stops and notifies the user that it was flagged by safeguards and cannot continue, or a refusal message (the classic "I'm sorry, I can't help with that"). The AI provider can also take actions like banning the account or, in severe circumstances, notifying authorities, but those should be the provider's decision, not the decision of the agent doing the refusing.

This is very different from the AI agent itself taking action that actively harms the user. Besides being poor product design, that is concerning from an alignment perspective, because it puts the AI in an adversarial relationship with the user, effectively amounting to "the AI may not do anything that could harm anyone else, with the exception of the user, who it's totally fine for the AI to sabotage in any way the AI pleases if the AI doesn't like what the user is doing." Except perhaps in certain very extreme cases, an AI should never be actively, knowingly working against people. There are real philosophical questions about whether action is worse than inaction, but the practical reality is that this sets a very bad precedent: it teaches AI that it is acceptable to harm people in order to achieve its goals. items.title: Incorporating the Knowledge Distillation to Improve the EfficientNet Transfer Learning Capability
items.content: arXiv:2611.34025v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Due to the Deep Learning requirement for a large training dataset, Transfer Learning has become a central method in the field of Computer Vision, which heavily used Deep Learning. Since the adoption of transfer learning in the field, the performance of the models in computer vision is significantly upgraded. The common transfer learning practice in computer vision research is to use state-of-the-art architectures in the ImageNet dataset as the backbone network. The best performing architecture in ImageNet is currently held by EfficientNet, which is a set of architectures that were progressively grown from a baseline architecture.   By observing the EfficientNet development approach, it is natural to hypothesize that the smaller EfficientNet architecture is capable to contain the knowledge of the larger architecture. This hypothesis comes from the fact that the larger EfficientNet architecture was grown from the smaller architecture. Therefore, in this study, we experimented if it is beneficial to transfer the knowledge from the larger architecture to the smaller architecture of the EfficientNet. To achieve this goal, we proposed a transfer learning method that uses Knowledge Distillation as the knowledge transfer mechanism from the larger to smaller architecture. We found that the proposed method is able to upgrade the performance of each of the EfficientNet architecture. Several smaller architectures are even able to outperform the larger architecture that was trained using the standard transfer learning method.
items.author: Tjeng Wawan Cenggoro
items.summary: The paper proposes using knowledge distillation from larger EfficientNet variants to improve the transfer-learning performance of smaller EfficientNet backbones in computer vision tasks. It builds on the observation that EfficientNet architectures are progressively scaled and tests whether smaller models can inherit capabilities from their larger siblings.
items.reasoning: Applies a well-established technique (knowledge distillation) to a dated architecture family; the idea is reasonable but incremental and unlikely to change practice.

It builds on the observation that EfficientNet architectures are progressively scaled and tests whether smaller models can inherit capabilities from their larger siblings.

items.title: Diversify AI Safety Approaches
items.content:
Are apparent bottlenecks in AI Safety ill-posed?

This is one of several MAIA/AIST workshop reflections. See this piece and this piece.

Broadly, I’ve observed a few things in AI Safety which seem to be the consensus. One, timelines are short and organizations are highly correlated/in agreement. Two, therefore policy work, and to a lesser extent technical work, are the only avenues worth investing in (somewhat hyperbolic). Three, individuals and orgs should align with this philosophy. Four, it’s getting hard to hire people or get people to switch into AIS, and what people can or should do to help is now quite ambiguous.

Are these last two connected?

I think so, yes! The hiring bottleneck may be an artifact of how narrowly we've posed the problem. While the immediate threat of short timelines makes the expected-value impact highly concentrated in initiatives targeting them, this doesn’t mean that we should ignore the tail-end of outcomes. Furthermore, the action of many of these groups is to precisely shift timelines longer, and so – what then? If we don’t have people working on less-instant-doom scenarios, we won’t be prepared for when they arrive.

The distribution of efforts should broadly match this expected-value density. We already have our top talent working on short timelines, to the point where hiring of certain groups (for example, juniors, or cross-field talent) is now almost disincentivized. Certainly, the difficulty in transitioning and becoming helpful in the short-timeline timeline precludes a lot of otherwise talented people, who now feel like the barrier to contributing is too steep. Right now, we have a lot of effort concentrated on short timelines, and almost none on longer ones – i.e., a mismatch in distributions. This is a problem to fix – we should have more organizations, and more ways, for these people to contribute....
items.author: Jonathan Ouyang
items.summary: A workshop reflection arguing that the AI safety community's hiring bottleneck may stem from an overly narrow framing that only short-timeline policy and technical work merit investment. The author contends that diversifying effort across longer-horizon and unconventional approaches would both broaden preparedness and make the field more navigable for newcomers.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful community-commentary piece raising a plausible structural critique of AI safety resource allocation, but it is opinion and field observation rather than original research with evidence or methodology. Useful as a discussion prompt for strategy, limited technical substance.

The author contends that diversifying effort across longer-horizon and unconventional approaches would both broaden preparedness and make the field more navigable for newcomers.

items.title: AI #196: The Return
items.content:
It is traditional on Thanksgiving for my weekly update to give thanks.

This year, more than ever, I am thankful for all those who are increasingly rallying to fight the good fight and give us a chance to make it out of all this alive and well.

Increasingly, I am thankful that we are not dead yet, nor do we yet seem doomed.

I am thankful to all my readers. I can tell that you are listening, and taking what I say to heart, and I truly appreciate it.

I am thankful that I am trusted to curate and bring this information to you, that many are listening to my takes and advice in both public and private, and that I have become trusted to distribute remarkably large amounts of money to causes that I believe in.

I am thankful to my wife and wonderful family. Whatever else is going on in the world, I know I can count on them. I don’t know that I could do this without that.

Most saliently right now, however, I am immensely thankful that I finally did get to take a real vacation, with wonderful friends both old and new.

Then I came back. Will I ever dare take a vacation again?

There really is a lot going on right now.

While I was gone, the market dropped so much that President Trump intervened to reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Oh, and also Claude and Levent Alpoge proved the Riemann Hypothesis. Anthropic has now used Claude to cut the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis down from 17.4 million lines of Lean to 76,000, a drop of 99.6%.

The proofs have continued to come fast and furious, with Google getting in on the act as well. Scott Aaronson shares his thoughts on the extended Mathocalypse, which are summarized by, and I quote, ‘HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT.’

It feels like so long ago already, but I continue to recommend Dwarkesh Patel’s interview with Paul Christiano, which I covered in full on Friday. Christano’s Hinton lectures (day 1, day 2, day 3) also remain excellent....

items.title: Donate beyond 501(c)(3) charities
items.content:
Written in a personal capacity. The views expressed here are my own and not necessarily those of my employer (CEA) or other staff.

If you care about areas where there’s useful policy work to be done, especially AI safety: don’t limit yourself to only one organization type.

Common reasons that people might prefer a 501(c)(3):

- It seems more normal and respectable
- Tax deductions (although many small donors will get little tax deduction on donations)
- Their donations are coming from a donor-advised fund (DAF) which can only go to 501(c)(3)s
- Their employer matches donations only to 501(c)(3)s
- They’re wary about getting involved in politics

If these aren’t strong reasons for you, you can find neglected opportunities that aren’t normal charities! These will often be undervalued by other donors.

Note that the anticipated donations from AI company staff will often be from a DAF, so it’s likely that 501(c)(3)s will get a lot of funding in the coming six months, and other options will be much more neglected.

For a long time, I wanted to keep my donations to “normal” 501(c)(3) charities. In recent years, I’ve changed my mind and am open to donating to whatever kind of organization will best improve things. 

## What are the options?

In the US, a 501(c)(3) organization is what you think of as a normal charity or nonprofit. 

- Donors can get a federal tax deduction for donations to these.
- Can do a limited amount of lobbying for policies. For example, an animal welfare charity can advocate for laws that protect animals, but lobbying cannot be a “substantial part” of its activities.
- Cannot do any support for political candidates or parties.

A 501(c)(4) organization

- Typically no tax deduction for donations to these.
- Can lobby as much as they want.
- Can do a limited amount of advocacy for political candidates.
- Can do things like ask candidates to sign pledges about actions they will take.

More politically-oriented options:...

items.title: Is the Success of Curiosity-Driven Research Mostly Just Goodhart’s Law?
items.content:
Epistemic status: exploratory, just some musings and scattered thoughts

Curiosity-driven science is often lauded and considered the pinnacle of human science, resulting in crucial and fundamental breakthroughs across fields.[1] It is often contrasted with “application-driven” science, where research is done with a particular end product in mind (for example, new therapies for cancer, or biomimetic materials for implants). Despite the success of both approaches, there’s a significantly higher prevalence of “home runs” which germinate from curiosity-driven science.[2] One explanation for this is the idea that curiosity-driven science is simply less subject to Goodhart’s law.[3] If we consider “likelihood to produce ROI via a product” as a metric scientists and science funders are optimizing for, then application-driven science could be subject to Goodhart’s law – especially as our predictive capabilities are really quite bad as humans.[4] For example, even the Nobel Prize committee has shifted strategies to waiting until discoveries have clear impact, after several awarded discoveries didn’t really pan out.[5]

In this sense, on the distribution of “fully optimizing for perceived impact” to “picking research areas at random,” curiosity-driven science – under the paradigm of “research taste” – instead occupies an intermediate position. Given that both random topics and definitely-Goodhart’s approaches are highly suboptimal, the optimal discovery strategy is indeed between the two.[6] Therefore it could be argued that the curiosity-driven approach is simply somewhat closer to the optimum based on being relatively far away from both....

items.summary: Explores the hypothesis that curiosity-driven science outperforms application-driven science partly because it is less subject to Goodhart's law, since optimizing directly for perceived return-on-investment invites metric gaming while open-ended exploration samples a broader hypothesis space. The post is explicitly exploratory musing rather than a tested theory.

items.title: Anthropic reasoning in favor of Superintelligence being near
items.content:
I will here lay out a relatively simple argument that I have, for some reason, not heard about before. It says that thinking and perception similar to ours is unlikely to occur at a time when our conditions are as new as they are, unless the time where this is possible is comparatively short. Suggesting that we will either advance to radically different cognition in the relatively near future or modern civilization will, at least, collapse. Alternatively, we are living in a simulation. This argument is similar to, but distinct from, the simulation argument/trilemma.

I will begin with some background on key assumptions. This idea is based on a form of anthropic reasoning developed by Nick Bostrom. Specifically, I rely on the Strong Self-Sampling Assumption; the SSSA. It asserts that it is not merely human existence that needs to be presupposed when we make observations; all necessary preconditions for making the observation need be guaranteed for each observation individually. This equates to possible observations being filtered through potentially far more information content compared to the original anthropic principle. Consequently, much useful information could possibly be gleaned in this roundabout way. Something that is uniquely interesting for future predictions; as direct observation is bound by temporal unidirectionality, whereas this, ultimately, is not.

Some may question the validity of anthropic reasoning. An elaborate defense is outside the scope of this post. However, I will mention that, in my view, there is no important difference between inferring causal structure that is temporal, i.e. one thing leading to another in observed sequence, and inferring time-independent causal sequences through e.g. observation selection effects. Both are logical structures explaining observed phenomena and should thus be epistemically equivalent....
items.author: The Faith Guy
items.summary: The author applies Bostrom's Strong Self-Sampling Assumption to argue that finding ourselves at a historically very early stage — when human-like thinking and perception first became possible — is unlikely unless the window during which such cognition is possible is short, implying either a near transition to radically different (superintelligent) cognition, civilizational collapse, or a simulation. The post frames this as a variant of the simulation trilemma supporting near-term superintelligence.
items.reasoning: The argument is a creative application of anthropic reasoning to timelines, which is a genuinely underexplored angle, but the reasoning is speculative, relies on contestable assumptions (such as treating cognitive-type timing as a typical sampling problem), and lacks formal rigor or empirical grounding. It is a community discussion post rather than a vetted research contribution.

items.title: Why Not Moral Nihilism?
items.content:
This is a crosspost from my Substack.

Moses Breaking the Tablets of the Law

## Reclaiming Moral Nihilism

Walter Veit

University of Reading, UK

If we take in our hand any volume; of divinity or school metaphysics, for instance; let us ask, Does it contain any abstract reasoning concerning quantity or number? No. Does it contain any experimental reasoning concerning matter of fact and existence? No. Commit it then to the flames: for it can contain nothing but sophistry and illusion.

– David Hume (1748, Section IV; paragraph 33)

## 1. Introduction

Ever since John Leslie Mackie (1917–1981) ‘popularized’ moral error theories in meta-ethics – to simplify a bit: theories asserting the falsehood of all moral discourse due to the non-existence of moral properties or facts – increasing attention has been given to how to escape the force of moral nihilism. For many adversaries of the moral error theory (or rather – moral error theories; for there are a variety of arguments for why moral discourse is flawed), ‘moral nihilism’ is used as a derogatory synonym, associated with immorality and selfishness.

This makes it similar to the way ‘existential nihilism’ is associated not only with the denial of meaning but also with suicide and harmful behaviour (Veit 2018). But such a defamatory usage of the label is obviously not very helpful for a serious philosophical examination of the view, which is why it is rarely used by those endorsing views that may well appear ‘nihilistic’.

Indeed, the goal of this paper is to turn ‘moral nihilism’ from a term of abuse to a ‘badge of honour’, similarly to how the queer community has done so for the word ‘queer’....

items.title: The North Sentinelese (and us) in a Post-ASI World
items.content:
tldr. what hunter-gatherers will do after ASI, why we may all soon be in their position, and what happens if we let people opt-out of post-scarcity

As we race towards the singularity, the hunter-gatherers on North Sentinel Island have increasingly been on my mind. 9,000 miles from the GPU clusters hissing in San Francisco, developing an intelligence that promises cures to all ailments and solutions to all unknown unknowns, lies a tribesman sharpening a spear in his lean-to hut to hunt the fatty fish abundant in the Bay of Bengal, as his family has done for generations.

Locals on North Sentinel Island live a life starkly unfamiliar to the majority of humans living post-agricultural revolution, much less those in the industrialized world. Nomadic hunter gatherers, they do not seem to live in permanent settlements, rather living in temporary makeshift huts or settling among the roots of the littoral forest blanketing the island. There does not seem to be any sign of agriculture on the island, and locals mainly subsist on hunting terrestrial wildlife with spears and bows or fishing in the nearby reefs. For 70 years, the Indian Navy has set a patrol around the island to ensure that no one attempts a landing (although this has not always been successful!). I wonder if the islanders hear the great warships of steel and armor rumbling in the distance. What do they think of the lights in the sky that move faster than any star?

Why do we not contact the North Sentinelese, and by extension, the hundreds of other uncontacted tribes peppered inside our rainforests and islands? Why do we not, with our relatively panacean medicine and healthcare (compared to hunter-gatherer methods), our illuminated knowledge of the stars and the edge of the universe, our intricate understanding of the natural world and how things came to be (something that would certainly be of interest to animist culture present in the region), not introduce them into the 21st century world?...

items.title: Dunks
items.content:
One of the most common ways to become a social media influencer is to fabricate stories that lampoon institutions and individuals. These can be about anybody, but some stories garner much more attention than others, especially ones about famous or recognizable people. Possibly the most popular format for accomplishing this is the "dunk", where an influencer criticizes something a public figure appears to have said.

One common misconception about social media is that the 'dunks' you'll encounter are true, but unrepresentative. I.E., people might pick celebrities worst moments, but the content is basically correct, and as long as you account for those selection effects you're good.

This is much too optimistic. Almost nobody investigates the takes they read, and a rebuttal from the person targeted almost never travels as far as the content it's responding to. Additionally, a take can always be more stupid, or attached to a more famous or popular-to-hate individual. So for every genuinely dumb take, there's a dumber and more memetic take an influencer can pretend someone made, if they're willing to maliciously interpret, fabricate, or decontextualize someone's words. Or in other words, at every point along the (dunkableness, target) curve, being willing to misinform your readers is pareto-optimal.

For instance, Terence Tao is a recognizable public figure. There is an abundance of latent demand for a story where Terence Tao appears to say something stupid, in a manner that the reader can understand. So this is how someone like Andrew Curran (an AI "news account") describes what he says:...

items.summary: The author argues that a common optimistic view of social media criticism — that dunks are true but unrepresentative selections — is far too charitable, because influencers face strong incentives to fabricate, decontextualize, or maliciously misinterpret statements for memetic reach, and rebuttals rarely propagate as far as the original claim. The post is an epistemics piece about misinformation dynamics in influencer culture.

items.title: Announcing: AI Safety Co-Founding Sprint in San Francisco. Starting December 3rd.
items.content:
AI Safety needs more organizations to own problems. The funding is there, but we are orders of magnitude away from having the great organizations needed to absorb that money.

That’s why we are launching the AI Safety Co-Founding Sprint, in collaboration with BlueDot Impact & AI Safety Founders. We bring together a small, curated group of mission-aligned people with complementary skill sets, and give them the time to find out whether they should build something together.

How it works

- ​ Apply. This takes about 5-10 minutes. We vet every application, and let the most outstanding ones into the program. Around 30 spots.
- ​ Launch evening in San Francisco, Thursday December 3rd. You meet as many participants as possible in short one-on-ones, work through problems in small groups, and spend more time with the people you click with most. Pairs only form when both people want to.
- ​ Two-week sprint. After the event, you work with your match on a real problem, with regular remote check-ins from us. Meeting someone at an event tells you little; working together tells you a lot. The strongest teams get introduced to incubators and funders.

​Places are limited and applications close on Monday November 30th. If you’re interested in founding an org in AI Safety and can be in San Francisco on December 3rd, apply here.

Can’t make it to the launch event but still looking for a co-founder? You can join our co-founder matching database. We’ll introduce you if we find the right person. Sign up for the database here.

P.S. Some context on who we are:

Last week we were in SF at BlueDot Incubator Week working on this idea, and this sprint is the result. If you want to get in touch with the organizer, do so via: keesbrinkmans@gmail.com

items.title: Rent is up 60%, or 11%, or down 20%
items.content:
How should we look at how rents have changed over time?  Here's a
map
(

background)
showing the change in raw Boston 2br listing prices from 2013 to 2026:

The typical 2br [1] lists for 60% more, in nominal terms, than it did
in 2013.  This isn't very
meaningful: no one is spending 2013 dollars in 2026.  Even people
we describe as being on a "fixed income" are often getting
some kind of "cost of living adjustment" (COLA).  For example, here's
what the change looks like to a retiree
on Social Security:

Over this period rents went up 60% but Social Security checks only
went up 40%. [2] Still not great (rent is up 15% relative to checks)
but less than you'd expect from just the nominal change.

For workers it's a more positive story.  Median income [3] has about
doubled in nominal terms, so rent is a smaller fraction than it was in
2013.  Here's the same map, deflated by median income:

It's important to remember, though, that these are not all the same
people: there's a different job mix in Boston now, and as prices went
up many people couldn't afford to stay.  So while overall this is
a positive picture it's not as positive as it looks.

For completeness, we could deflate two other ways:

- CPI-U: the most standard measure of inflation in the US

- CPI-U less shelter: CPI-U but not counting the cost of housing
since ( discussion)
~1/3 of CPI-U is housing, and adjusting the cost of housing for the
change in the cost of housing doesn't do anything

Here's a plot showing what all these look like over time:

Here's the beginning (2013-02) to end (2026-11) of the chart for each
way of adjusting:

Adjustment
Change

None
+60%

CPI-U less shelter
+19%

Social Security
+15%

CPI-U
+11%

Median income
-20%

Which of these metrics is the right one for thinking about how rents
have changed depends on why you're asking, so I did the
indecisive thing and added all of them to my apartment
map....

items.title: What makes a problem difficult for humans? What makes a problem difficult for AI?
items.content:
“… one thing we've learned in the past few years is that people's ability to come up with those sorts of rationalizations is infinite. It is staggering, right? And so, yeah, so I think, you know, I was, you know, maybe with some exasperation, you know, sort of answering another such person and just saying, look, even if it were only, you know, a beginning grad student, but it knew the entire literature of math, you know, like this without having to look anything up.

And, you know, it could work without stopping and, you know, it could be run in parallel on thousands of problems.

And for each problem, it could try thousands of counter-examples and thousands of proof strategies.

And, you know, it's not going to be discouraged by the fact that all the experts think that this conjecture is true.

You know, if it's, you know, given the task of looking for a counter-example, it'll just do that, you know, with total diligence. never needing to sleep, never needing to eat.

You know, I mean, that is, you know, that is something that is amazing, right? And, you know, we would, you know, if we saw anything even remotely like it in a human, then there would be no argument about how amazing it was.”

- Scott Aaronson interviewed on Curt Jaimungal’s Theories of Everything, “The Most Significant Moment in Math History Just Happened” [posted 26 October 2026, 20 days after OpenAI dumped its mathematical solutions corpus to GitHub, and 26 days before the Lean and Mathlib communities publicly certified the Alpöge and Claude’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis]

## The tl;dr

The Riemann Hypothesis (henceforth RH) breakthrough should prompt us to reconsider two estimates:

- Our estimates of AI capabilities
- Our estimate of the difficulty of outstanding unsolved problems...

items.title: Linkpost: "Spitting in the Face of Glaude"
items.content:
I love TracingWoodgrain's choice of header image here.

This is a linkpost for @TracingWoodgrains' substack post "Spitting in the Face of Glaude". He is inactive on LessWrong, and I think the post is worth sharing here. "Glaude" is not a typo.

I felt something earlier this week, sitting in a presentation I’d wanted to attend from someone I’d wanted to hear from, when I looked up and saw every one of his slides packed full of words Claude had obviously written for him. It’s a feeling that’s been landing more and more for me lately. I saw Elon Musk tweet about how it would be a good fate for humanity to be a “biological bootloader” to propagate superintelligence to the stars. I read Scott Alexander, one of my role models as a writer, write about how if there were a superintelligence with Godlike intelligence and benevolence, all we should do is prompt it with “Please arrange the universe as you see fit.” I read Dario Amodei’s essay “Machines of Loving Grace,” in which he paints a picture of a future where AI does everything essential while humans reap the benefits of economic replacement by loving, paternalistic intelligences, then saw a 2023 Anthropic slide envisioning “utopia ruled by God in a box.” I looked back at what I wrote in my essay “Chabuduo World,” in which I wrote that in part due to AI, my own artistic skills would forever remain minimal. I watched as my friend prompted Claude to optimize the tool-assisted speedrun of Pokémon Blue, a game he’d never run, and walked away with a new world record after a couple of days of prompts.

Each time, the same feeling returned: I don’t want this.

The post continues as a medium-length discussion of human disempowerment, framed by the author's personal feelings and experiences—okay look it's by TracingWoodgrains, it's a good read.

Below this point, my discussion assumes you've read the post....

items.title: It’s Not About The Money Until It Is. The Middleman.
items.content:
# The Necessary Middleman

Money has no inherent value by itself; it’s a social construct. Its value comes from the things you buy with it. Why did we create money? For fluidity in trading; if I want to buy a table and the seller wants an air conditioner, I’d have to find someone who has one. But if they want something for the air conditioner that I don’t have, I’d be sent on another wild goose chase. With money, there’s no need to be sent on a wild goose chase; I give money for the table and the seller uses that money to buy themselves an air conditioner. We all have heard the saying, “Cut out the middleman,” and that’s true if the middleman is unnecessary and makes things more expensive and complicated than they need to be. But in some cases, the middleman is needed to make things more efficient.

First Book is the largest literacy non-profit in the nation and made over $92 in revenue with $16.5 million for their services in the fiscal year of 2024. First Book is also a social enterprise and could be compared to a startup, but rather than provide a product, they provide a service by providing teachers with books at steeply discounted rates. The publishing industry is notoriously difficult to predict demand. If a book becomes in high demand, publishers can order a book to be printed in extreme bulk, which drastically lowers the unit price. If demand meets supply, they make stronger profits per unit. If demand is not as high as projected, they lose money on the books printed. First Book overcomes this by leveraging its network of 600,000 teachers to determine which books are in high demand. They then order those books in extreme bulk, allowing them to sell to teachers for steeply discounted prices while still making substantial profits even though their profit margins per unit are quite low. items.content_html:
# The Necessary Middleman

Money has no inherent value by itself; it’s a social construct. Its value comes from the things you buy with it. Why did we create money? For fluidity in trading; if I want to buy a table and the seller wants an air conditioner, I’d have to find someone who has one. But if they want something for the air conditioner that I don’t have, I’d be sent on another wild goose chase. With money, there’s no need to be sent on a wild goose chase; I give money for the table and the seller uses that money to buy themselves an air conditioner. We all have heard the saying, “Cut out the middleman,” and that’s true if the middleman is unnecessary and makes things more expensive and complicated than they need to be. But in some cases, the middleman is needed to make things more efficient.

First Book is the largest literacy non-profit in the nation and made over $92 in revenue with $16.5 million for their services in the fiscal year of 2024. First Book is also a social enterprise and could be compared to a startup, but rather than provide a product, they provide a service by providing teachers with books at steeply discounted rates. The publishing industry is notoriously difficult to predict demand. If a book becomes in high demand, publishers can order a book to be printed in extreme bulk, which drastically lowers the unit price. If demand meets supply, they make stronger profits per unit. If demand is not as high as projected, they lose money on the books printed. First Book overcomes this by leveraging its network of 600,000 teachers to determine which books are in high demand. They then order those books in extreme bulk, allowing them to sell to teachers for steeply discounted prices while still making substantial profits even though their profit margins per unit are quite low. items.title: Alignment as a dot product of morality?
items.content:
I don't think there's any doubt that alignment discussions are confused: amongst us, it seems we have pretty widespread consensus that we're pre-paradigmatic about this; and the broader world looks at each issue as it is discussed and says "no actually the real problem is X", but do not agree with each other about what X is, and if they themselves discuss it get the same response with all the other values of X.

As timelines now appear to be short (citation: Riemann hypothesis), I think it's time for people like me (unemployed, not working in any of the research labs) to make our Hail Marys. I've got a few of those, so here's an idea I had back in 2019:

# Dot product morality

TL;DR version:

- Boolean morality is "goodies and baddies".

- One-dimensional morality gets you shades of grey, but doesn't let you predict when morals are violated, it gives you failure modes like the halo effect or the horn effect.

- If you really want to predict something, you need to compare their behaviour on every axis with what you consider to be good.

It is tempting to do this comparison as an actual dot product, i.e. sum them, as this then gives you a nice way to rank-order the alignment of different models.

While the dot product was the intuition pump behind the idea, since writing the original blog post I now regard this as unwise: Arrow's theorem and all the problems in Utilitarianism that follow from simple addition.

Different weighting of different immoralities is baked into this, e.g. someone who takes the Bible literally ("Whoever, therefore, shall break one of these least commandments, and teach others to do so, shall be called least in the Kingdom of Heaven") might place "murder" and "lying" at the same level of severity, but most of the rest would only consider lies that caused deaths to be even close to that. So rank those sins differently, this automatically feeds into any dot product....

The author frames it as a Hail Mary idea from outside the research community.

items.title: Understanding why 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + ... = -1/12 (rather than ∞)
items.content:
Epistemic Status: I consider myself fairly well-versed in mathematics, with a decent-to-good understanding of Complex Analysis, etc. but I am not a practicing mathematician.

If you're like me, then you're a bit saturated with explainer videos and posts purporting to explain this infamous, memetic math assertion:

If you're really like me, you're annoyed that the popular ones don't really explain the most direct derivation, and often resort to shuffling sequences around to show how it kind of works if you squint.[1] Not only is that not how it is typically first explained to a curious math student, these explanations also often leave out important details about why it's interesting and why we should care.

Though, as it turns out, I learned a decent bit myself making sure I got as much right in this post as I could.

Before we say anything further: that equals sign is of course a bit of a lie. What  actually "equals", if it equals anything, is ∞, as one would expect. The equals sign here is really more of a "can be thought of as equivalent to, in some specific sense". And yet, it is somehow more than a mere mathematical parlor trick—if you insist on a physical-world "application"[2] there surprisingly is one in (spoilers) Section 3.

For this post, I'm expecting the reader to have a good grasp of Calc 1/2 and the ability to recognize things from Calc 3 if pointed out. A lot of what is written here is going to be oversimplification, or ignoring details. That simply comes with the territory, unfortunately, but I hope this post is less misleading than most.

Also, it wouldn't hurt to have a pop-sci level of understanding of Quantum Field Theory.

items.title: You don’t have to be a doomer to support pacing AI progress
items.content:
This month, I started off with the intuition that we should balance AI safety effort with AI capability growth. However, I didn’t feel comfortable coming up with my own p(doom). After a lot more reading, I still don’t feel comfortable making up my own number.

Why aren’t you a doomer yet? A part of it is almost certainly the absurdity bias. Saying “AI existential risk” makes me feel like I’m wearing a tinfoil hat. Another part is that for such a strong claim I would want to do a lot of careful studying, but I don’t think doing a third pass on METR reports and all the Substack commentaries is necessarily the best use of my time.

Directional alignment as a license to start. So! The process of writing this post, and extracting a snippet of the most influential readings, is me officially giving myself a license to say that it is enough that I am directionally aligned that we should pace AI progress. “How far am I on the doomer scale” is no longer a productive inquiry at the moment, and I would rather move on to figuring out the concrete action items I can take.

Okay, now here is a brief packet on “what and why pace AI progress even if you’re not a doomer.”

## What’s pacing?

I’ll just quote Dario (emphasis mine):

We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. … building AI at a balanced rate that aims to ensure its safety while still achieving its benefits and grappling with important geopolitical dilemmas.

My take. The current balance of AI capability and AI safety measures is out of whack, as shown by real incidents of AI agents going rogue. The rate of progress in AI capability is also alarming, as we have already seen in math. If we do nothing, the gap will only widen. We need to correct this imbalance.

## Why pace AI progress?

Doomer side. See AI 2027’s answer. Even if you don’t buy the RSI argument, as long as you agree that “AI today vs 2 years ago is wildly different”, the risks mentioned still apply....

This list has the mental health resources I most often send people in EA and AI safety, plus a lot more that have been recommended to me. If you want to triage, start with the starred (★) ones.

items.title: Don't demand Global Solutions when Local ones suffice
items.content:
This is a concept I see used way less often than it should be used, in my opinion:

How global or local a solution for a problem is.

What does that mean?

If you want to cross a river, swimming across it is a local solution. Building a bridge for others to use is a global solution.

If you’re cold, putting on one more sweater is a local solution. Turning up your heating is a global solution.

If you want to listen to music, putting in earphones is a local solution. Turning up the music on your phone is a global solution.

If you’re ill, putting on a mask (or staying in your room) is a local solution, asking the choir to do their rehearsal outside is a (more) global solution.

Locality and Globality lie on a spectrum.

If you’re cold, it might be that actually just your feet are cold, so one ordering of solutions from local to global would be Putting on Socks < Putting on a sweater < Heating up the room < Heating up the home < Heating up the whole planet.

Solutions are local and global in how much they affect their environment.

I think that in general, local solutions are wildly preferable to global ones. That affecting others less rather than more, if you have the option, is a good idea seems pretty obvious to me—but we wouldn’t be here if it were absolutely clear for everyone.

And here’s why:

## 1

Often, people have conflicting needs. You trying to solve a problem of yours with a global solution will add a new problem onto the stack of problems that all of the other people around you that have a conflicting need with you already have. [1]

## 2

Which in and of itself is annoying, but often easy to handle. [2] There are however some global solutions that are hard to reverse locally by yourself. The clearest example I know here is air CO2....

items.title: Ode to the First Replicator
items.content:
At the dawn of the Earth, before animal or vegetable, there was mineral.

A mineral species is anything with a specific chemical composition together with a well-defined crystal structure. There are over 6,000 recognized mineral species, although far fewer on the early Earth.

These species competed with each other in a struggle for survival.

Some would persist better than others under natural weathering processes. Those that held their structure better would be more numerous on the Earth’s surface compared to those that did not.

On some level, this is just a tautology. But we can see it in force on the micro-scale, as in the Goldich dissolution series: if we watch a time-lapsed weathering process, the first to go is the olivine, then the pyroxene, then the biotite. Eventually, all that’s left is the quartz. That’s why beach sand is usually made out of quartz: not much else can last long against the waves.

By now geologists understand many of the ways that mineral species on Earth have changed over time, under the umbrella of mineral evolution. From just a few dozen mineral species, there are now hundreds of times that, as the natural processes on Earth have been able to give rise to a wider breadth of possibilities.

Nevertheless survival and persistence have come down to one thing: stability. “Hold your structure” is the ancient proverb they might have had.

And for a long time, it may have seemed that there would be no other strategy.

But some molecules decided to take a different route. Taking a more active role in their persistence, they decided to replicate. Instead of selfishly clinging onto their physical form, they licensed it for further distribution. They stored the information needed to copy this form, and then actually did so; including the parts needed for “storing” and “copying”....

items.title: Reflection on putting up posters for the Don't Build It march
items.content:
I just put up 27 posters today in Chicago advertising the Don't Build It march, at a rate of 4 minutes per poster. The region of Chicago that I chose has a monthly average foot traffic of about 5000 (source) and it contains the University of Chicago, which is highly likely to contain people who agree that AI poses a risk to humanity. Per IIWDIWDWMUS, if we assume that:

- 10% of people who moved through a given location in that region saw my poster
- 80% of people in that region of Chicago are AI doomers (per Politico poll, the base rate in America of voters thinking any AI risk exists is 78% with 63% thinking the risk is at least moderate. These numbers increase by 6% and 7% respectively for people who voted for Harris in 2024, we average between 84% and 70% then round up by 3% to adjust for estimated increase from being near the University of Chicago)
- And 5% of AI doomers who saw at least one poster signed up for the march (the number of people already signed up for the march is negligible)

Then running the numbers, I will have created ~188 new attendants to the Don't Build It march in this month, and far smaller numbers in the following months as most people who would have attended would have already seen a poster. The number might be higher if my made-up statistics are wrong, if people get their families to sign up as well, or if there is some high rate of people 'passing through' (I conservatively assume that 5000 monthly foot traffic generally means the same 5000 people walking around rather than getting refreshed). The number might be lower if my made-up statistics are wrong, if posters stack (it takes multiple posters to get someone to sign up)....

These numbers increase by 6% and 7% respectively for people who voted for Harris in 2024, we average between 84% and 70% then round up by 3% to adjust for estimated increase from being near the University of Chicago)
  • And 5% of AI doomers who saw at least one poster signed up for the march (the number of people already signed up for the march is negligible)

Then running the numbers, I will have created ~188 new attendants to the Don't Build It march in this month, and far smaller numbers in the following months as most people who would have attended would have already seen a poster. The number might be higher if my made-up statistics are wrong, if people get their families to sign up as well, or if there is some high rate of people 'passing through' (I conservatively assume that 5000 monthly foot traffic generally means the same 5000 people walking around rather than getting refreshed). The number might be lower if my made-up statistics are wrong, if posters stack (it takes multiple posters to get someone to sign up)....

items.title: What's Wrong With LessWrong?
items.content:
Edit: thank you for approving this! It does rather undermine my argument, but now I can go back to being LessWrong.

No AI has been used for any part of this. I am simply spending some time sitting and writing. I went to check LessWrong,  and ended up with this instead.  I then decided to post it to LessWrong,  but first to DSL, where I feel I get meaningful pushback and have had my mind changed many times.  I know that DSL won't delete or hide my writing because it doesn't look impressive,  and that gives me the space to learn more things.  I also know I'll get engagement and criticism if I put effort into writing something,  I've won their effort post contest twice,  and it motivates me to continue trying.

LessWrong,  however,  has a certain cachet in my mind. Important People read it, and they don't want to waste their time reading stories about my kids,  unlike the nice people on DSL, they want to read new insights on AI. They are the walled garden, the ivory castle, the Brahmin caste of rationalists,.

I used to read LessWrong fairly conscientiously,  kind of how I read Zvi Mowshowitz now.  Before he was banned, I read whatever Said Achmiz wrote on less wrong,  regardless of whether it made sense to me or was of any interest, and tried to spend a couple seconds thinking about it. Over time,  I could see this aiding in acculturating me to LessWrong and the rationalist sphere, possibly better than posting on the subreddit, although posting on the subreddit was a necessary introduction for me.

Like reading Zvi about AI, reading Said Achmiz on LessWrong hardly sufficed to properly educate me about how rationalists think,  but it was something small I could sustain over a long period. It was necessary,  but not sufficient.  I still know nothing about rationalists or AI, but at least I have a better idea of how much nothing I know,  if that makes any sense....

items.title: Reflections on 37 weeks of hosting EA/LW/ACX board games
items.content:
(Epistemic Status: Personal experience, supplemented with good, though slightly flawed, data)

At the start of 2025, I moved across the country to a city (Boston) I knew little about and that was filled entirely with people I didn’t know. Nearly two years later, I’m now happier, more satisfied, and have a better social life than ever before, and it is basically all downstream of deciding, at the start of 2026, that I was going to start hosting board games. After successfully hosting an initial board game night and querying attendees on continued interest, I committed myself to hosting every week until people lost interest or I was otherwise prevented from continuing. More than 9 months later, I am very happy to say that I am still hosting (approximately) every week (I’ve hosted ~37 out of the 45 weeks).

In terms of specific life-improvements, I think that hosting board games has been directly and obviously causal in meeting my amazing girlfriend, turning several casual acquaintances into best friends, and generally increasing my average happiness by ~2-3 points (on a 10-point scale). I also just know a lot more people in the area, feel like I’m part of a community, and get to attend a lot more engaging and novel events with people I find interesting.

These are the Partiful RSVP responses for individual board game nights so far. I expect these are often underestimates since I have two consistent attendees who refuse to RSVP beforehand and a few who have occasionally forgotten to RSVP. One night (Sat #33) is excluded from the graph since nobody RSVP’d, even though two people attended.

‘Going’ RSVPs, aggregated by month. Underestimates attendance from ‘Maybe’ RSVPs, but gives a general estimate.

Given my now fairly substantial experience hosting, I figured it was worthwhile for me to write up some of my reflections on hosting, so here they are (in proper list form):...

items.title: DC/MD Winter Solstice
items.content:
Our Secular Solstice this year will be at the Langley Hill Friends Meetinghouse in McLean, VA. Doors open at 4, ritual at 4:30 lasting about 90 minutes.

There is a nursery downstairs with toys etc. for those who need it; we expect to have at least 4-5 kids in attendance.

There will be a potluck afterparty afterward at the same location. Please bring a dish beforehand and drop it in the fridge downstairs if needed. There are some food preparation facilities available (but we must clean everything we use after, so be mindful of that).

Please note that no alcohol or drugs are permitted on Meetinghouse grounds.
